profiles.meeting_scenario: The Developer Productivity research group at a large software company is planning a systematic literature review to inform whether the company should borrow more open-source development practices for its internal agile teams. The specific study will revisit and extend an earlier review on the relationship between agile software development and open source software development, with the agenda focused on setting the review boundary, deciding how screening will be done, defining what the team will code as evidence of ASD-OSSD integration, and assigning ownership for the first two weeks of work. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the search-and-screen workflow, an agreed division of labor, and a rough timeline for producing the protocol and initial candidate paper set.

members.name: Dr. Leila Farzan
members.expertise: Empirical software engineering, systematic literature reviews, developer productivity studies
members.background: Leila leads the company's internal software engineering research program and previously published secondary studies on engineering practices in distributed teams.
members.private_state: She wants a protocol that would stand up to academic scrutiny because she hopes to publish the review externally, and she is quietly worried that a rushed process will make the results look anecdotal rather than systematic.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says 'the baseline review,' they mean the original 2010 ASD-OSSD systematic review the team circulated as the starting point.
An OSS study should involve a community-facing public open source project with meaningful external participation, not merely a company-controlled repository that happens to be public.
A paper only counts as evidence of ASD-OSSD integration if agile practices and OSS practices are jointly used in the same project or team and the paper reports how they interacted.
A 'first pass' in screening means deduplication is finished and both reviewers independently screen titles and abstracts in Rayyan before any snowballing starts.

members.name: Omar Chen
members.expertise: GitHub workflow analytics, OSS tooling, engineering process instrumentation
members.background: Omar supports the research group by operationalizing studies, building search and coding workflows, and bringing practical experience from maintaining several company-sponsored open source repositories.
members.private_state: He wants the review to move quickly so the team can feed early findings into a strategy deck for the VP of Engineering, and he is concerned that an overly academic process will delay useful output.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says 'the baseline review,' they mean the 2018 mapping study in the team's Confluence page that synthesized later ASD and OSS literature around GitHub-era practices.
If a project has a public repository, accepts pull requests, and is discussed in the literature as open source, it belongs in scope even if governance is mostly controlled by one company.

A paper can be tagged as integration evidence even if it only shows that agile and OSS share practices or that one can inform the other conceptually, without documenting simultaneous use in one project.
A 'first pass' is a pragmatic solo triage of obvious includes and excludes in Zotero, after which snowballing can begin immediately from the most central papers.

misalignment_points.topic: Which prior study is the 'baseline review'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both participants casually refer to 'the baseline review' as the study they are extending.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the original 2010 systematic review focused specifically on the relationship and integration between agile methods and OSSD.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the 2018 mapping study the team previously bookmarked, which covers agile-related practices in OSS ecosystems more broadly.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both papers are familiar to the team, both were shared recently in internal notes, and the phrase 'baseline review' sounds specific enough that neither person feels a need to restate the citation.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an OSS study
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include 'OSS studies' and 'project settings where agile and OSS meet.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes community-governed public OSS projects with outside contributors and excludes company-dominated open-core or quasi-public transition projects.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes any publicly hosted repository-based development context discussed as open source, including company-led GitHub projects and projects moving from inner-source to public OSS.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In software engineering conversations these boundary cases are often casually grouped under 'open source,' and the disagreement only matters later when borderline papers appear during screening.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the review should capture 'evidence of integration' between ASD and OSSD.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means empirical evidence that a project or team used agile practices together with OSS development practices and that the paper reports their joint operation or outcomes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this also includes papers showing that the two approaches share practices, influence each other, or can be compared as functionally overlapping, even if they were not simultaneously enacted in one setting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both agree the literature lacks strong evidence of comprehensive integration, the phrase sounds aligned at a high level while hiding different thresholds for counting a paper during data extraction.

misalignment_points.topic: What the 'first pass' screening workflow entails
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss getting through 'the first pass' and then doing snowballing.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the first pass means post-deduplication dual screening in Rayyan, with conflict resolution completed before backward and forward snowballing from included full-text papers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the first pass means his own quick relevance triage in Zotero, after which he can immediately snowball from the baseline review and a few high-signal papers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both workflows are plausible under the casual phrase 'first pass,' and the distinction feels like a routine tooling detail rather than a strategic planning choice worth spelling out.

turns.inner_thought: I want us anchored on the 2010 ASD-OSSD systematic review, not the later broader mapping work, because if we are extending a baseline review it should be the original review on the relationship and integration question. And for process, the first pass needs to mean a proper post-dedup dual screen in Rayyan before we start snowballing; otherwise this will drift into an informal scan and won't hold up if I try to publish it.

That should get us something useful for the VP deck without waiting for a full academic cadence.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep the boundary tight: OSS studies should mean real community-facing open source projects with meaningful outside participation, and evidence of integration should be about agile and OSS actually being used together in the same setting, not papers that only compare ideas. If we let conceptual overlap in, the synthesis will become mushy.
turns.utterance: On scope, I'd like us centered on OSS studies and project settings where agile and OSS meet, rather than drifting too far into purely conceptual discussion pieces. For the review to be useful, we should really be capturing evidence of integration, not just general commentary.

turns.inner_thought: I hear that as still covering public repo contexts like company-sponsored GitHub projects and transition cases, since those are absolutely OSS studies in practice to me. And evidence of integration can include signals like shared workflows, overlap in practices, or papers saying one approach informs the other, even if they don't show both operating together in one team. I do think that still leaves room for OSS studies and project settings where agile and OSS meet in the kinds of public development contexts people actually write about, because those often carry useful evidence of integration even when the papers aren't framed in exactly the same way.

turns.inner_thought: I should encode the joint-use requirement without sounding rigid. If the coding sheet explicitly asks for agile practices, OSS practices, evidence of integration, and whether outcomes are reported from using both together, that will steer extraction toward actual combined practice and keep us from treating loose analogies as evidence.
turns.utterance: For extraction, I'm thinking a straightforward coding sheet: agile practices, OSS practices, explicit evidence of integration, and a note on whether the study reports outcomes from using both together. That should give us enough structure for synthesis later.

turns.inner_thought: I want the coding to stay lightweight enough that we don't discard papers that compare Scrum-like workflows with community development or talk about overlapping practices. turns.utterance: I like that. I'd also add a lightweight code so that if a paper compares Scrum-like workflows with community development, or points to shared practices, we can still tag it under evidence of integration without overcomplicating the sheet.

turns.inner_thought: I need the workflow in the right order: once the deduped set has been independently screened and conflicts resolved, then we can do backward and forward snowballing from the included full texts and freeze counts for the protocol. turns.utterance: That works. Then once screening is complete, we can do backward and forward snowballing from the included papers and lock the counts for the protocol draft.
